opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting directions for us, and the intuition is fairly simple. In physical AI, there are two capabilities you really want a model to have. One is understanding: looking at a video or a scene and reasoning about what's happening, why it's happening, and what is likely to happen next. The other is generation: imagining how the world will evolve, rendering a plausible future given some action or condition. For a long time, people treated these as separate problems with separate models. But they are two sides of the same coin. Both require an internal model of how the physical world works.

So how can they help each other? Let me start with the reasoner helping the generator. A generative model can produce videos that look beautiful frame by frame but violate physics. Objects pass through each other, liquids behave strangely, a robot arm grasps something that should have slipped. A reasoner that understands physics can act as a critic. It can look at generated outputs and say, "This part doesn't make sense," and that signal can be used to filter data, provide rewards, or guide generation toward more physically consistent results. In a sense, the reasoner becomes the judge that keeps the generator honest.

The other direction is equally important. The generator can help the reasoner. A reasoner needs a lot of data, especially data about rare situations, edge cases, and counterfactuals: what would happen if the car turned left instead of right, or if the box were heavier. Collecting that in the real world is expensive and sometimes dangerous. A good world generator can synthesize those scenarios, and the reasoner can learn from them. Beyond data, generation can also be a form of thinking. When humans reason about the physical world, we often simulate in our heads. We picture the cup falling before deciding where to put it. A generator gives the reasoner the ability to "imagine" before it answers.

When you put these together, you get a loop. The generator proposes possible futures, the reasoner evaluates them, and the feedback improves the generator. The better generator produces richer training signals and imagined scenarios, which improves the reasoner. If this loop works well, the two capabilities can bootstrap each other, somewhat like how self-play helped game-playing systems improve beyond the data they started with.

Of course, there are real challenges. You have to be careful that the two don't reinforce each other's mistakes. If the reasoner has a blind spot and the generator learns to exploit it, you can drift away from reality. So grounding in real-world data remains essential. The loop has to be anchored by real observations. But conceptually, I believe unifying understanding and generation is a key step toward world models that are truly useful for robots, autonomous vehicles, and other physical AI systems.

r002.rationale: The response describes generation helping the reasoner through synthetic scenarios and imagination, but does not mention propagating generator gradients back to improve the reasoner’s learned representations.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it gets at why we built Cosmos the way we did rather than as two separate projects.

Let me start with the basic picture. The generator is a world model in the classic sense — you give it a state and an action, and it predicts what happens next, as video, as sensor data, as the physical consequences of that action. The reasoner is the part that looks at a situation, understands it, and decides what to do. Historically, those have been trained and improved largely independently. The insight behind Cosmos 3 is that each one is actually the best teacher the other could have.

Take the direction from generator to reasoner first. The hardest problem in physical AI is data. You cannot collect enough real-world experience of a robot dropping a glass, or a car encountering a child running from behind a bus, to train a reasoner on those situations. But a good generator can produce those situations on demand, and crucially, it can produce the counterfactuals — what would have happened if the reasoner had chosen differently. So the reasoner gets to practice in a space that is far richer than any dataset, and it gets feedback on decisions it never actually made in the real world. That's the thing reinforcement learning has always wanted and rarely had for physical systems.

Now the other direction, which I think people underestimate. A generator trained purely on video learns correlations. It will produce things that look plausible but violate physics in subtle ways — an object that passes through a table, a liquid that doesn't conserve volume, a hand that grips something without any contact. The reasoner, because it has to actually act on those predictions and succeed, is very sensitive to those errors. When the reasoner's plan fails inside the generator's simulation in a way that it would not fail in reality, or vice versa, that mismatch is a training signal pointing at exactly where the generator's physics is wrong. The reasoner is effectively probing the generator for its weaknesses, and those weaknesses are the ones that matter for action, not just for making pretty videos.

So you get a loop. The generator expands the reasoner's experience. The reasoner sharpens the generator's fidelity in the places that actually affect decisions. And the thing that makes this more than a nice story is that both models share the same underlying representation of the world. That's the architectural choice that makes the loop tight. If the reasoner thinks in terms of abstract symbols and the generator thinks in pixels, the mismatches are hard to translate back into gradients. When they share a latent space, a disagreement between them is directly actionable.

I'll be honest about where we are. We have seen clear improvements on both sides in the domains where we've closed this loop — manipulation, driving, some industrial settings. What we have not yet shown is that the loop keeps compounding indefinitely, or that it transfers cleanly to domains with very long horizons where small physics errors accumulate. That's the open question. My bet is that it does, because the real world is the ultimate ground truth, and every time you deploy, you get a chance to correct both models at once. But I'd rather tell you that as a hypothesis than as a result.

r002.rationale: The response mentions shared latent space and actionable disagreements, but does not say that propagating generator gradients back to the reasoner could improve its learned representations.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is in creating a feedback loop between reasoning and generation. The reasoner can help identify what a generated world should contain, how events should unfold, and where something is inconsistent. That gives the generator more useful guidance than simply asking it to produce something that looks realistic.

In the other direction, the generator can give the reasoner scenarios to explore. If the reasoner predicts that an action will lead to a certain outcome, generating that scenario can help expose assumptions or suggest alternatives. So generation becomes a way to explore “what if,” while reasoning helps evaluate what was generated.

The key challenge is grounding that loop. Agreement between the two doesn’t necessarily mean they’re correct—they could reinforce the same mistake. You need checks against observations or physical constraints. With that grounding, I think there’s a real opportunity for each component to provide better training signals for the other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is in creating a feedback loop between the two. The generator can produce a possible future—what might happen if a robot takes a particular action—and the reasoner can examine that future: Is it physically plausible? Does it achieve the goal? What should change? That feedback can help the generator produce more useful predictions.

In the other direction, the generator can give the reasoner more experience to learn from. You can generate different situations, vary the conditions, and explore outcomes that would be difficult to collect in the real world. The reasoner then has an opportunity to improve its understanding of actions and consequences.

The important part is grounding that loop in reality. If both models share the same misconception, they can reinforce it. So the opportunity is to let generation and reasoning improve each other while using real-world evidence to check whether they are actually getting better.
